description_ru: Вымышленная новость о группе туристов, застигнутых метелью, и ночи, проведённой в снежной пещере.
text:
Six hikers who were missing for almost thirty hours on the fictional Mount Corrigan were found alive and well on Sunday morning, after one of the largest mountain rescue operations in the history of the region. The group, which consisted of four adults and two teenagers, had been caught in a sudden snowstorm on Friday afternoon. According to the rescue team, they survived the night by digging a shelter in the snow and sharing a single flask of tea.

The hikers had set out from the village of Lower Ashby at eight o'clock on Friday morning. The weather forecast, which had been checked by the group leader, a schoolteacher named Priya Hargreave, had promised clear skies until the evening. By two o'clock, however, the temperature had fallen sharply and a thick cloud had rolled in over the ridge. Ms Hargreave later told reporters that visibility had dropped to a few metres within ten minutes, and that she had realised at once that they would not be able to follow the path.

Instead of pressing on, the group decided to stay together and look for shelter. A fifteen-year-old member of the party, Callum Birtwhistle, who had been studying survival skills at school, suggested digging a snow hole. "I'd only read about it," he said, "but I remembered that you have to make the entrance lower than the sleeping platform, so the warm air stays inside." Using two small shovels and a cooking pot, the hikers dug for nearly three hours, taking turns to rest.

Back in the village, the alarm was raised at seven o'clock that evening, when the group failed to return. Volunteers from the Ashby Mountain Rescue Team, who were already on call because of the weather, set out within the hour. The search was hampered by winds that were said to have reached eighty kilometres an hour, and helicopters were grounded until the following morning. Team leader Desmond Okonjo-Reid said that the volunteers had searched through the night with torches, calling out the names of the missing.

Inside the snow hole, meanwhile, the hikers were fighting to stay warm. They huddled together, wrapped in spare clothes and foil blankets, and took turns to clear the entrance whenever it was blocked by drifting snow. Ms Hargreave said that the teenagers had been the bravest of all. "They never complained," she said. "At about three in the morning, one of them started singing, and soon we were all singing, badly, which kept us awake." The party had agreed that nobody should fall asleep for more than twenty minutes.

At first light on Sunday the wind dropped, and a helicopter spotted a small orange flag that the hikers had planted on top of their shelter. A rescue crew was lowered to the ridge, and the six were reached shortly after nine o'clock. Doctors at the regional hospital examined them and reported that two adults had mild frostbite on their fingers and that one teenager was suffering from exhaustion, but that no one was seriously hurt. All six were allowed to go home the same afternoon.

Mr Okonjo-Reid praised the group for the decisions they had taken. "People often make the mistake of walking on in the hope of reaching safety," he said. "This group stayed put, kept calm, and made themselves easy to find. That is exactly what we recommend, and it is almost certainly the reason they are alive today." He added that the rescue team would like to remind walkers to carry spare food, a torch and a whistle, and to leave details of their route with someone at home.

The rescue also drew attention to the equipment the group carried. Besides the flask of tea, they had two foil blankets, a head torch, a small first-aid kit and a bag of chocolate biscuits, which the party shared out in tiny pieces. A paramedic who met them on the ridge said that the biscuits had probably made a real difference, because the body burns food to produce heat. He added that the hikers had also swapped wet gloves for dry socks, a trick that he described as unusual but extremely clever.

The incident has prompted a debate about the safety of the popular mountain, which attracts more than fifty thousand visitors every year. A local councillor, Eleanor Whitcombe-Jones, has suggested that warning signs should be installed at the start of the main paths, and that a weather station should be built near the summit. Others disagree. A farmer who has lived at the foot of the mountain for sixty years said that signs would not help people who ignored the sky. "The mountain doesn't care what the notice says," he remarked.

Callum, whose hands were wrapped in thick bandages, was celebrated as a hero in his village on Sunday evening. When asked by a reporter whether he would ever return to the mountain, he thought for a moment and replied that he certainly would, but that next time he would pack a bigger flask of tea. The headteacher of his school has said that survival skills will remain on the curriculum.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Короткий краткий звук между «а» и «э», рот открыт слабо; не «о».
Губы округлены вперёд, без касания зубами; не путайте с «в».
Ударение ставьте на нужный слог: ударный слог длиннее, громче и выше по тону, остальные сокращаются.
Задняя часть языка к мягкому нёбу, звук идёт через нос; не добавляйте «г» в конце.

questions.question: How did the hikers survive the night?
questions.answer: They dug a snow hole and kept warm together, taking turns to clear the entrance.

questions.question: Who suggested digging the shelter?
questions.answer: Callum, a fifteen-year-old, who had studied survival skills.

questions.question: What does the rescue leader advise people to do in a storm?
questions.answer: Stay put, stay calm, and make themselves easy to find.

questions.question: What did the farmer say about warning signs?
questions.answer: The mountain does not care what the notice says; signs do not help people who ignore the sky.
